solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Scrounge a large one

parts.note: to bum a cigarette is to scrounge one
per = a, as in 'ten pounds a head'

explanation.surface: Someone cadging a big helping of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'a' is worth PER, while the article in 'a large one' belongs to the definition, so the clue splits after 'Scrounge a'.
explanation.definitionFit: Bumper is used as a noun for anything unusually big of its kind, a sense most familiar from bumper crop or bumper issue.

clue.text: Postwar child peeled tropical fruit that's seen in Australia

parts.note: a baby boomer, born in the postwar birth surge

indicators.note: peeling fruit strips away its skin, so the outside letters of the fruit's name come off

parts.note: MANGO without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A baby boomer eating a peeled mango somewhere in Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is only a loose description, but the boomerang is the object most associated with Australia; the mango fits the tropical north, which helps the disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by association: the Aboriginal throwing stick is an emblem of Australia, so it is the thing you would expect to see there.

clue.text: Police on radio evacuated transit network

parts.note: the Met is London's Metropolitan Police

indicators.note: an evacuated building has had everyone inside cleared out, so the word keeps only its shell

parts.note: RADIO with its middle letters removed

explanation.surface: Police radioing about the evacuation of an underground railway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' is a placing word here: in a down clue the police piece sits on top of the radio piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Metro is the general word for an underground city railway, taken from the Paris Métro.

clue.text: Sudden insight: northbound Tube convenient when dropping daughter

indicators.note: in a down clue north is up the grid, so a northbound word is read from the bottom
to drop something is to let it fall away, so the daughter's letter falls out of the word

explanation.surface: A commuter's flash of inspiration: the northbound Underground is handy for the school drop-off.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital T on 'Tube' makes you think of the London Underground, but it is just a pipe. Dropping a daughter off at school is part of the surface's school run.
explanation.definitionFit: An epiphany is a moment of sudden revelation, a sense extended from the Christian feast of Christ being revealed to the Magi.

clue.text: Controlling figure succeeded; very English — The Greatest!

parts.note: Muhammad Ali called himself The Greatest

explanation.surface: A sports headline hailing a triumphant English champion as the greatest.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface's triumph is a red herring; 'succeeded' is the one-letter abbreviation. Svengali is the hypnotist in George du Maurier's novel Trilby.
explanation.definitionFit: A fictional name turned common noun: after du Maurier's mesmerist, a svengali is anyone who manipulates and dominates another.

clue.text: Roughly 4 hour wait finally for buck

indicators.note: something handled roughly is knocked about, so the letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: the answer to 4 across, used as fodder

indicators.note: finally means at the end, so only the last letter of the next word is used

explanation.surface: A four-hour wait for a dollar, or for a male deer.
explanation.walkthrough: '4' is a cross-reference to 4 across, not the number, so the fodder is that answer. 'Buck' suggests a dollar or a stag; here it is gym equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: A gymnastics sense: a buck is a short padded block on legs that gymnasts vault over, a smaller version of the full-length horse.

clue.text: Visiting Namibia on vacation, ordered blue Crab for one

indicators.note: a visitor stays inside someone else's place, so the rearranged letters go inside the other piece
to order things is to arrange them, so the letters are rearranged
a place on vacation has been vacated, emptied of its contents, so only the outside letters remain

parts.note: anagram of BLUE, placed inside NA

explanation.surface: A blue crab turning up in Namibia on holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital C is the tell: this is the Crab Nebula in Taurus, not a crustacean.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Crab Nebula, remnant of a supernova, is one instance of a cloud of gas and dust in space.

clue.text: Art Basel reeling after mag exposed material used in column

indicators.note: reeling means staggering about, so the letters stagger into a new order
in a down clue, coming after means sitting below the earlier piece
exposed means stripped of covering, so the word loses its outer letters

parts.note: MAG with its outer letters removed

explanation.surface: A magazine exposé leaves the Art Basel fair reeling after a column on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Column' pretends to be a magazine column, but it is a stone pillar. Art Basel is an international art fair held in Switzerland.
explanation.definitionFit: Alabaster, a soft white stone easy to carve, has long been worked into pillars, so the definition describes a use rather than giving a synonym.

clue.text: Peace-loving inspiration finds herself in dire need

indicators.note: in marks the answer as lying inside the words that follow, running across the gap

parts.note: the letters run across the word break, dropping the outer D and D

explanation.surface: A pacifist muse discovering she is in desperate straits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Herself' confirms a female answer, hidden in d-IRE NE-ed. Irene (Eirene) is the Greek goddess of peace.
explanation.definitionFit: A mythological sense: Eirene was the goddess who embodied peace, and her name is simply the Greek word for it.

clue.text: Large sighs heard following umpire's decision

indicators.note: what is heard is the sound, so the word is replaced by one that sounds the same

parts.note: a cricket umpire gives a batsman out

indicators.note: following means coming after, so this piece goes second

explanation.surface: A crowd sighing heavily after an umpire gives a batsman out.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leads and reads as an adjective on 'sighs', which hides it well.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, used mostly of clothing: outsize garments are extra-large ones.

clue.text: Hemlines and belt tailored to capture masculine finishing touch

indicators.note: tailoring cuts and reshapes cloth, so the letters are cut and reshaped
to capture is to take inside, so the letter goes within the others

parts.note: m = masculine, captured inside the anagram

explanation.surface: A dressmaker adjusting hemlines and a belt as a final flourish.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue stays in the sewing room, so the definition blends in; 'and' is only surface glue between the two fodder words.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: an embellishment is a decorative addition, the kind of detail added last to finish a piece off.

clue.text: One leaving Italian region, say, reflected resentment

indicators.note: something leaving goes away, so that letter departs from the region's name
a reflection in a mirror reads backwards, so the letters reverse

explanation.surface: An emigrant leaving Umbria looks back with bitterness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is the usual signal for an example, EG, which then reverses.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, usually met in the phrase to take umbrage, meaning to take offence.

clue.text: Return to manage hotel for a period

indicators.note: to return is to go back the way you came, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: H = hotel in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Coming back to run a hotel for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return to manage' reads as a comeback to management, but 'to manage' is the verb COPE, reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, with the flavour of a distinctive era, as in a geological epoch.

clue.text: A vote introduced by British PM for disused weapon

indicators.note: to be introduced by someone is to be brought in by them, so the vote goes inside the PM's name

parts.note: taken as written, goes inside ATTLEE
a cross on the ballot paper

explanation.surface: A British prime minister bringing in a vote on an old weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'PM' could be any premier or the afternoon; Attlee, Labour prime minister after the Second World War, is the one whose name fits. The word lives on for a formidable woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A historical sense: the broad-bladed war axe went out of military use centuries ago, so it is fairly called disused.

clue.text: A style of dress worn by geek back to front, hence the rush?

indicators.note: back to front means reversed, so the word is read from its end
clothes worn by someone sit alongside them, so the dress piece is put next to the geek piece

parts.note: an A-line dress flares from the shoulders or waist

explanation.surface: A geek wearing a dress back to front, and the thrill that follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A style of dress' reads as one phrase, but the A is split off and an A-line dress is still needed after the reversed geek.
explanation.definitionFit: A metonym: the thrill of excitement is called an adrenaline rush after the hormone behind it, so the rush can stand for the hormone.

clue.text: File blunder in Times article on Bush?

parts.note: a rasp is a coarse file

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another, so the blunder goes inside the multiplication word

parts.note: as in 3 by 4 = 3 times 4; ERR goes inside

explanation.surface: A newspaper story on President Bush's gaffe, filed in The Times.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital T makes 'Times' a newspaper, but it means multiplied by. The definition is a pun: the fruit grows on a bush, and a raspberry is also the rude noise one might blow at Bush.
explanation.definitionFit: A cryptic description: the berry is an item that hangs on a bush, and the question mark admits the double reading.

clue.text: Stop big name in NYC sport making a comeback

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so the name comes back the other way

parts.note: the Mets, New York's baseball team

explanation.surface: A plea to halt a New York sports star's return.
explanation.walkthrough: The New York Mets are a Major League Baseball team, a big name in the city's sport.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb synonym, used of flows: to stem the tide or stem the bleeding is to stop it.

clue.text: Curative network set up to support wealthy Florentines

indicators.note: in a down clue, set up means raised, so the word is read upwards
a support holds something up from beneath, so in a down clue this piece goes below

explanation.surface: A healing network established with Florentine money.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay reads in the opposite order from the surface: the family comes first in the answer even though the network is named first in the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain adjective synonym: medicinal and curative both describe something with healing power.

clue.text: Photo of biscuits fresh from the oven?

explanation.surface: A picture of just-baked cookies.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark covers the image of snaps that are hot. Biscuits is the British word for cookies.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a snapshot is an informal, quickly taken photograph.

clue.text: My waterproof shoe? A pound wasted

indicators.note: something wasted is thrown away, so those letters are discarded

parts.note: GALOSH loses A and L (pound, from libra)

explanation.surface: Someone lamenting a pound spent on a rubber overshoe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' reads as a possessive, but it is the exclamation, as in 'My, how you've grown!'
explanation.definitionFit: Two interjections of mild surprise that can replace each other: 'My!' and 'Gosh!'.

clue.text: With which to direct cast delivering line?

definitions.meaning: the surface wants a director guiding actors; an angler's cast is the throw, and the rod aims it
not an actor delivering a line of dialogue, but the fishing line being sent out over the water

explanation.surface: A theatre director guiding the cast through their lines.
explanation.walkthrough: Cast, delivering and line all belong to the stage, but an angler casts the line and uses the rod to direct it.
explanation.definitionFit: Read as angling, the whole clue describes the rod: the tool that directs a cast as it sends out the line.

clue.text: Drive empty Bugatti into swimming pool

indicators.note: an empty car has nothing inside, so the word keeps only its outside letters

parts.note: a lido is a public open-air pool

indicators.note: driving into something puts you inside it, so this piece goes inside the pool

explanation.surface: Someone driving an empty Bugatti into a swimming pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drive' seems to start the car story but is the noun: sex drive.
explanation.definitionFit: A psychological sense: libido is the sex drive, so drive in that sense is a fair synonym.

clue.text: US newspaper owner, drug dealer, carrying about 454 grams?

indicators.note: about can mean turned around, as in about-turn, so the letters reverse
a dealer carrying goods holds them on his person, so the weight goes inside

parts.note: 454 grams is 1 LB, written ILB and reversed

explanation.surface: An American press baron exposed as a dealer carrying a pound of drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 454 grams must first become '1 lb', with the digit read as I.
explanation.definitionFit: An American usage: on a US paper the publisher is the owner or chief executive, not merely the firm that prints it.

clue.text: Roly-poly pudding for starters topped with fruit

indicators.note: starters come first, so only the first letter is used
in a down clue, topped with puts the named piece above

explanation.surface: A roly-poly pudding with fruit on top.
explanation.walkthrough: Jam roly-poly is a British rolled suet pudding, which makes 'Roly-poly pudding' look like one dish; here roly-poly is the definition, meaning chubby.
explanation.definitionFit: Two adjectives for a pleasantly round figure: a roly-poly child is a plump one.

clue.text: Global outbreak has Democrat fleeing in terror

indicators.note: to flee is to run away, so those letters run out of the word

parts.note: PANDEMIC loses DEM, short for Democrat

explanation.surface: A pandemic sends a Democrat running scared.
explanation.walkthrough: DEM is the usual short form of Democrat; the surface's fear is exactly the answer, which makes the definition easy to overlook.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: panic is terror that takes over and makes people act wildly.

clue.text: Breaking news: yellow regularly ignored in material

indicators.note: breaking into something means forcing a way inside it, so these letters go inside the other piece

parts.note: news as the plural of new, N N

indicators.note: ignoring at regular intervals skips every other letter

parts.note: Y, L, O: the first, third and fifth letters of YELLOW

explanation.surface: A news bulletin that skips the yellow in a fabric report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking news' reads as a TV banner, but 'Breaking' tells the yellow letters to break into the news.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: nylon is one kind of material, the synthetic fibre used for stockings and rope.

clue.text: Elevate university commendation

explanation.surface: A university honour that lifts someone up.
explanation.walkthrough: A plain charade: the definition comes first and the pieces follow in order.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary verb synonym: upraise is an old-fashioned way of saying raise up.

clue.text: Troop formation has no shelter retreating, Switzerland admitted

indicators.note: troops retreating go backwards, so the letters run backwards
someone admitted is let inside, so the country code goes into the reversed letters

explanation.surface: Troops caught without cover pulling back and taking refuge in Switzerland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has no shelter' reads as a plight, but NO and LEE are both used as letters, and CH goes after the first E.
explanation.definitionFit: A military sense: an echelon is a stepped formation in which each unit is set back diagonally from the one ahead.

clue.text: City of Olympus almost ruined prominent couple from Thebes

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the last letter is dropped
the prominent part of a word is its front, so the first two letters are taken
something ruined is wrecked, so the letters are wrecked into a new order

parts.note: the two leading letters of THEBES

explanation.surface: Two famous Thebans lament a ruined city on Mount Olympus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'City of Olympus' looks like the definition, but the city is only 'City'. Plymouth is a port in Devon, England.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by class: Plymouth is a city in south-west England, famous as the Pilgrim Fathers' port.

clue.text: Uptight, nursing temperature, oxygen off the scale

indicators.note: nursing means holding close, like a baby in the arms, so the other letters go inside

explanation.surface: A tense patient with a fever and on oxygen, their readings off the charts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off the scale' sounds like extreme readings, but it means music not written in any key.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical pun: atonal music abandons key, so it is literally off the scale rather than extreme.
